item.title: Capitol agenda: GOP trifecta sputters into final days
item.description: Some GOP lawmakers openly wonder what their party will get done before the end of the year under renewed pressure from the White House to ram through a swath of stalled priorities.

media:content.media:title: From left, Sens. James Lankford (R-Okla.), John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), and John Thune (R-S.D.) look on during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Republicans wanted to check off a list of policy goals before Democrats took over Congress. They’re hitting some major hurdles instead.

Senate Republicans emerged from hours of meetings Wednesday without a clear path to advance another party-line spending bill. Chances have also dimmed on confirming some of President Donald Trump’s executive branch nominees.

And House Republicans, unable to even proceed through regular floor business due to attendance issues, have cut their legislative workweek short.

It’s all left some GOP lawmakers openly wondering what their party will get done before the end of the year under renewed pressure from the White House to ram through a swath of stalled priorities.

“I don’t know if we’re going to do anything,” Sen. John Kennedy said of his chamber, except confirm judges. “But everything else, I have no idea what we’re going to do.”

Here’s where the major agenda items stand:

— RECONCILIATION 3.0: Senate Republicans insist they aren’t closing the door on another party-line bill, but many are skeptical it will come together.

Even if it does in the Senate, House GOP leaders are unlikely to have the votes to adopt it given how many members are MIA after losing their elections.

— YEAR-END STAPLES: GOP appropriators made the case during their closed-door meeting Wednesday to hold off on reconciliation for now to allow government funding negotiations to proceed, several senators said after the meeting. Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed as much but declined to say how much time Republicans would give the bipartisan government funding talks.

Lawmakers appear far from consensus on government funding as the Dec. 11 shutdown deadline approaches. Also waiting for floor action: the annual defense policy bill and the farm bill.

— TRUMP’S NOMS: Committees have until Dec. 1 to advance any nominee they want to have included in a bloc of Trump picks set to be confirmed en masse next month, but there are signs of GOP pushback against some nominations that could keep them out of the package.

The White House also surprised senators by pulling Heidi Overton to lead the FDA, and other nominations have hit snags.

What else we’re watching: 

— SCHUMER'S LAST STAND? While Chuck Schumer fights to remain Democratic leader in the Senate, a big question remains about what he’ll do in two years. Schumer’s Senate term expires in 2028, and interviews with Democrats in New York and Washington suggest that moment could mark the end of his accomplished career one way or another. Some believe he will retire, and others are urging him to. Otherwise, they warn, he risks a bruising, potentially career-ending primary. In a statement responding to questions about his future, Schumer touted his record of delivering billions of dollars for New York through decades of challenges — like 9/11 and Covid.
 
— FINAL SENATE PERMITTING STRETCH? Senators will try again Thursday to pass a landmark bipartisan permitting reform deal after two Democrats Wednesday held up the legislation aimed at streamlining energy projects. Negotiators will now look to resolve outstanding disagreements and secure a timing deal for amendment votes and final passage as soon as Thursday. Sens. Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley did not consent to a time agreement necessary for lawmakers to proceed to amendment votes Wednesday, spokespeople for their offices confirmed.

Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney, Mia McCarthy, Chris Sommerfeldt and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.

item.title: A US attorney warned Dems about their Trump rhetoric. Legal experts say ignore him.
item.description: A Texas prosecutor says lawmakers’ plans for aggressive oversight could cross a criminal line.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Robert Garcia, who is slated to chair the House Oversight Committee, was one of five Democratic lawmakers who received letters.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
A federal prosecutor says he’s pre-investigating potential future crimes by Democratic lawmakers who might one day abuse their oversight powers.

The notion is so farcical it should simply be ignored, say six experts in congressional power and constitutional law.

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the Trump-appointed top prosecutor in south Texas, sent letters to four senators and a House member — all Democrats expected to wield powerful gavels in January — suggesting that their vows to aggressively investigate President Donald Trump’s allies could lead to criminal probes and charges.

Veterans of executive-legislative clashes say Reitz’s letters are legally meritless. There’s simply no crime, they say, when a member of Congress describes possible future oversight actions — even aggressive or controversial ones. And when they take the majority, those lawmakers’ investigative actions would be protected by one of the most powerful immunities in government: the Constitution’s speech or debate clause.

“They’re saber-rattling, but there’s no force behind the saber,” said Stan Brand, a former House general counsel under Speaker Tip O’Neill, who said Democrats should disregard the letters and avoid “adding a patina of legitimacy to what is essentially crackpot legal practice.”

Reitz’s letters to the five lawmakers — Sens. Elissa Slotkin, Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthaland Adam Schiff, as well as Rep. Robert Garcia — have raised eyebrows in Washington for the suggestion that lawmakers’ pre-election comments about investigating Trump allies could amount to criminal intimidation.

Democrats targeted by Reitz have vowed to push forward with their investigations and reject his attempt to criminalize what they say are their constitutional rights and duties. On Wednesday, Slotkin in a post on social media urged him to “bring it on."

"If there's a legal case to be made that you should prosecute someone for freedom of speech, do it. Come get me," Slotkin said in a video.

The Justice Department has stood by Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz and aide to outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, defending the substance of his letters.

“Oversight is not a license to threaten private citizens for exercising their First Amendment rights,” the Justice Department said in a statement that cited the same criminal statute referenced by Reitz. “Congress gave DOJ the authority to investigate those who willfully deprive people of their constitutional rights.”

But legal experts say the Hill shouldn’t sweat it.

“I’d largely ignore it and not give it air,” said one white collar attorney who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he previously represented Trump allies. A second attorney who has been active in congressional oversight matters said the latest spate of attacks from the White House and Justice Department is “even more laughable than usual.”

“Congress has extremely broad latitude to conduct oversight of the executive branch, and … the Speech or Debate Clause provides Congress, its committees, its members, and its staff (when functioning at the direction of the members) with a shield against any executive branch efforts to impede that oversight,” said Steven Huefner, an Ohio State University law professor who spent five years in the office of the Senate’s legal counsel from 1995-2000. “I therefore think that Congress can ignore the recent threats.”

Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown University law professor, said Reitz’s letters are “so clumsy and over the top” that they would be unlikely to provoke a serious legal clash between the branches. He said serious challenges to Congress’ authority are likely to develop later, once Democrats begin exercising their oversight power.

“It has seemed inevitable since long before Election Day that the Trump administration would take an incredibly combative approach against any efforts on Congress’s part to exercise even traditional forms of oversight over the executive branch,” Vladeck said. “The odds that, somewhere along the way, that approach provokes novel and serious Speech or Debate Clause issues seem as high as the odds that they’ll provoke novel questions about executive privilege, Congress’s legitimate investigative powers, and everything in between.”

Reitz said in a statement Tuesday that he’s simply following “the facts and law” by sending letters that ask lawmakers to preserve relevant documents.

After a left-leaning group filed a bar complaint against him this week, Reitz vowed to “continue my preliminary inquiry unfazed: to determine whether certain members of Congress have unlawfully stepped outside the legitimate legislative purpose of their planned committee activities, and to ensure Americans’ constitutional rights are protected.”

At the heart of the administration’s position are two longstanding principles: All congressional investigations and subpoenas must be tethered to a “legitimate legislative purpose,” and the Constitution’s speech or debate clause — intended to protect lawmakers from intimidation or coercion from the executive branch — applies only to a “narrow” slice of core legislative activity and not to broader conduct by lawmakers, like media interviews or subpoenas issued for improper purposes.

“I have taken routine, pre-investigatory steps to conduct a preliminary inquiry into certain members of congress for their statements vowing to weaponize committee activities against private citizens and entities associated with President Trump,” Reitz said in a statement, describing his letters as being sent “in coordination with Main Justice.”

A Justice Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the department’s internal deliberations, said there was nothing amiss about Reitz’s pre-review of potential oversight abuses.

“Sending threatening letters to Americans for associating with the President — before those officials have oversight power — is a clear attempt to chill associational rights and speech,” the official said. “And, yes, it is a valid exercise of DOJ’s prosecutorial power to prevent ‘anyone acting under the color of law to willfully deprive a person of their constitutional or federal rights.’”

Reitz’s letters have gotten some public backup from Trent McCotter, the Department of Justice’s second-in-command, who echoed the claim that the senators’ comments could violate Trump allies’ First Amendment rights. “DOJ will defend against threats to those rights,” McCotter wrote on X.

Reitz’s letters followed a similar missive from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is slated to lead the House Oversight Committee in January. Scharf’s letter borrowed language from a federal criminal statute to warn the California Democrat against aggressive investigations.

“[T]hreats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality,” Scharf wrote.

Though constitutional law experts say DOJ’s position is unlikely to clip Congress’ oversight ambitions, the battle for public opinion is another matter. Trump, they noted, has effectively countered congressional probes and impeachment efforts by pointing to Democrats’ own commentary and casting the investigations as “lawfare” or “weaponization” against him and his allies.

Through that lens, the attacks from the White House and Justice Department could be more effective. The administration’s letters point to loose comments from incoming House Democrats about raining down subpoenas like “Mardi Gras beads” or imploring Trump allies to “lawyer up.” Garcia jokingly described his future oversight plans as the result of “pettiness,” a comment that Scharf and Reitz both seized on.

Those comments could cost Democrats public support, some experts say, and also form the backbone of the administration’s litigation strategy against subpoenas they claim are not tied to a “legitimate legislative purpose.”

But the messaging fight is unlikely to translate into legal victories, they say. Though courts have paid attention to stray comments from Democrats during previous investigations, they have almost uniformly affirmed Congress’ broad power to obtain information.

So long as lawmakers embrace a plausible legislative purpose for their probes, “it is not a court’s ‘function’ to invalidate a congressional investigation,’” U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden wrote in 2021, ruling in favor of a House effort to obtain Trump’s tax returns.

McFadden, a Trump appointee, acknowledged comments from top Democrats, like House Ways and Means Chair Richard Neal and then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, had muddied the picture, but the judge said even mixed motivations are not enough to undercut Congress’ power.

That principle has held in more than a century of battles between the branches, during which courts —including the Supreme Court — have repeatedly held that the motives of individual members simply can’t overcome the will of the House or a legislative committee when pursuing a legislative goal.

“I wouldn’t dignify this with some counteroffensive in court,” Brand said of Congress’ response to the Trump administration letters. “If these guys try to enforce, it’s going to get flushed.”

item.title: The Republican trifecta is sputtering in its final days
item.description: Thin margins, attendance issues and stalled negotiations are adding up to a challenging lame-duck session.

media:content.media:title: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (right) and other top Republicans have yet to commit to attempting a costly GOP-only spending bill.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Jennifer Scholtes, Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Republicans want to run through the tape in their final weeks in power on Capitol Hill, but they’re hitting some major hurdles.

With 17 working days left in the Senate before Democrats take charge, Republicans emerged from hours of meetings Wednesday without a clear path to advance a party-line spending bill the White House desperately wants — just as several of President Donald Trump’s nominees hit snags that threaten to keep key roles filled by acting officials for two years.

House Republicans, meanwhile, are simply spinning their wheels. Leaders announced Wednesday they would cut their workweek short because of attendance issues.

It’s left some GOP lawmakers openly wondering what their party will get done before the end of the year beyond seating more Trump-appointed judges and, they hope, averting a government shutdown. The Senate is aiming to pass a bipartisan permitting reform bill this week, but it faces a more uncertain path in the House, which is also sitting on a bipartisan college sports bill the Senate passed months ago.

“I don’t know if we’re going to do anything,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said after emerging from one of the Senate GOP’s closed-door meetings Wednesday. “I think we’re going to continue to confirm judges, I’m pretty sure of that. But everything else, I have no idea what we’re going to do.”

Across the Capitol, one House Republican granted anonymity to speak candidly said there are “very low odds” Republicans will be able to enact any bill through the filibuster-skirting reconciliation process — especially given how many members have stopped coming to work after bruising election defeats.

“It’s dereliction of duty,” the Republican said, adding leaders would need to “publicly shame” colleagues “by name” into showing up.

The reality check comes as House and Senate Republicans have been under renewed pressure from the White House to use the waning days of their governing trifecta to ram through a swath of stalled GOP priorities.

As they met and reelected their leadership team after the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Senate Republicans agreed to a nonbinding resolution saying they would seek to "maximize" their remaining time in power — including confirming every possible nominee, passing “core” GOP priorities and attempting another reconciliation bill.

The party-line bill, in particular, is easier said than done. Trump has demanded $350 billion in military spending be included because Democrats are dead-set against supporting any funding that could further the war with Iran.

But many GOP senators, while publicly supportive, have long been privately skeptical it will come together. For one thing, Republicans still haven’t fully agreed on the scope of the hypothetical measure — $350 billion is more than many budget hawks can stomach.

For another, the Senate math gets harder for the GOP next month when incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio is sworn in after winning a special election to finish out the term of Vice President JD Vance, lowering the GOP’s majority to 52.

“Everybody recognizes it's going to be a herculean effort to try to get the House and the Senate to agree on the scope and the process,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said Wednesday.

Besides the GOP-only bill, legislators also need to worry about advancing three other typically bipartisan year-end staples: the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill and a measure to fund the government past a looming Dec. 11 funding deadline.

GOP appropriators made the case during their closed-door meeting Wednesday to hold off on reconciliation for now to allow government funding negotiations to proceed, several senators said after the meeting. Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed as much but declined to say how much time Republicans would give the bipartisan government funding talks.

Republican senators are also discussing whether to bring a spending package to the floor that would combine two fiscal 2027 bills: one funding veterans affairs and another funding the Pentagon, according to three GOP senators and aides granted anonymity to describe private conversations.

But Democratic votes will be needed to make this tactic work — and Democrats are not likely to support bankrolling the Pentagon without Iran restrictions and a guarantee that nondefense programs would get a funding increase, too.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said it would put Democrats on the spot: “Are they willing to work with us or not? And this makes them answer that question.”

Republicans are having success confirming Trump’s judicial nominees, with some vowing not to leave town this week until they have cleared a batch that has been teed up for votes. But some of the president’s other nominees are facing less certain prospects.

Committees have until Dec. 1 to advance any nominee they want to have included in a bloc of Trump picks set to be confirmed en masse next month. But there are signs of GOP pushback against the nominations of Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office and Kari Lake to be ambassador to Jamaica, among others, that could keep them out of the package.

The White House also surprised senators by pulling Heidi Overton to lead the FDA, and HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) declined to move forward with a top science nominee who was supposed to get a committee vote.

Republican leaders were also struggling to get things done in the House this week, with leaders unable to begin floor debate on two GOP-sponsored bills after 14 House Republicans didn’t show up to vote Wednesday. Eleven were nonreturning members.

Those attendance problems aren’t expected to get better: Outgoing House members had to vacate their offices and relocate to cubicles this week, further demoralizing defeated GOP incumbents who would just as soon close out their terms back home.

The upshot is that House GOP leaders are unlikely to have the votes to adopt any reconciliation measure that comes over from the Senate. Most House Republicans wanted the Senate to take up a framework they passed before the midterms instead.

House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), for instance, threw cold water on the likelihood of approving Trump’s full $350 billion defense request.

“I don't believe that you can win over enough budget hawks,” he said in an interview. “That’s my concern.”

Calen Razor and Katherine Tully-McManus contributed to this report.

item.title: GOP Rep. Nick Begich survives blue wave
item.description: The Alaska Republican hung on even as the GOP lost a Senate race and the governorship.

media:content.media:title: Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich is the sponsor of a bill that would blacklist foreign fishing vessels that illegally fish in U.S. waters.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
GOP Rep. Nick Begich III fended off an independent candidate who had the backing of the Democratic apparatus to hold onto Alaska’s sole House seat — becoming one of the rare Republicans facing a serious challenger to survive the party’s midterm bloodbath.

Begich, who aligned himself with Donald Trump despite the president’s unpopularity, narrowly prevailed over Bill Hill and two other candidates after a ranked-choice tabulation Wednesday, even as Democrats flipped other statewide offices in reliably red Alaska.

He’ll serve next year alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democrat he defeated to win the House seat just two years ago, after she ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The scion of a prominent Alaska political family also succeeded in a year that saw his uncle, Democrat Tom Begich, drop out of the governor’s race after finishing second in the August primary to consolidate support behind another Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who went on to win the governorship.

Hill, meanwhile, extends independent candidates’ midterm losing streak, joining a number of independent Senate candidates who lost red-state races to Republicans this year. House Democrats’ campaign arm had added the educator and commercial fisherman to its coveted “Red to Blue” program. But Eric Hafner, a perennial candidate who is serving a prison sentence in New York, was the sole Democrat listed on the ballot and still siphoned votes.

Democrats have won 257 seats to 172 for the GOP, with a half-dozen races left to be called.

item.title: Laurel Lee makes bid for top Republican on House Judiciary Committee
item.description: The Florida Republican is a former prosecutor and judge.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Laurel Lee (R-Fla.) departs a House Republican Conference meeting at the Capitol Hill Club in Washington, Sept. 18, 2024.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Laurel Lee has formally announced her bid Wednesday to lead Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee — a position that would have her going head-to-head with Democrats who could decide they want to impeach President Donald Trump.

“I understand the constitutional grounds for impeachment, the limits of congressional authority, and the difference between a policy disagreement and an impeachable offense,” said the Florida Republican in a letter to colleagues, obtained by POLITICO. “I am prepared to make those distinctions in the hearing room and explain them to the public.”

In her letter, Lee highlights her experience as a judge, federal prosecutor and Florida secretary of state to make the case that she can “distinguish allegations from evidence, apply the law fairly, and explain consequential decisions clearly.”

She also told her colleagues that she would be well-equipped to combat the wide range of investigations that committee Democrats — led by incoming Chair Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) — are already telegraphing.

If recommended for the post by the House GOP Steering Committee, Lee, who was elected to Congress in 2022, would be among the few Republican women in leadership roles in the chamber. She is expected to be competing against Reps. Lance Gooden (R-Texas) and Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.) for the position.

item.title: Van Hollen calls for AI safeguards amid leadership push
item.description: Failure to address AI risks would replicate the mistakes of the 1990s, the Maryland Democrat said.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks during the Senate Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies hearing on Capitol Hill on May 12.

item.dc:creator: By Sam Sutton
item.content:encoded:
SAUSALITO, California — Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said that setting guardrails around artificial intelligence would be a top priority if he succeeds in his challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats next year.

“The bottom line here is, we can’t take the same attitude toward AI that too many people took to Big Tech in the 1990s, which is that: ‘It’s inevitable. It’s out of our control,’” he said during a remote “fireside chat” at a Hewlett Foundation event. “That is a bunch of nonsense.”

The severity of AI-related cybersecurity risks, along with its rapid emergence as a driving force of economic growth in the U.S., has hastened calls for incoming Democrats majorities to move swiftly to head off potential threats. In his remarks, Van Hollen said that AI companies must “understand they’re going to be fully liable for any harm they cause” — even in instances where rogue agents fail to cause material harm. He also cited workforce-related issues as a concern.

“In a democracy, all of us should help develop the rules that help nourish our communities, and not simply allow it to go to folks who are trying to make a big, big buck,” he said.

In addition to targeting large AI firms, Van Hollen also said that he would prioritize policies targeting the role of private equity in youth sports, health care and the acquisition of small businesses. He also said that lawmakers should “go after” surveillance pricing techniques.

Schumer addressed AI risks himself Wednesday, lambasting President Donald Trump and his administration for not acting more decisively in light of the recent disruptions to critical digital infrastructure.

“We need to ensure the safe development and deployment of AI, or we’re going to see more outages and, God forbid, even catastrophic events going forward,” he said in a floor speech.

item.title: Lauren Underwood elected vice chair of House Democratic Caucus
item.description: The 40-year-old former Health and Human Services official beat California Rep. Sara Jacobs.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.) arrives for a press conference at the U.S. Capitol, Nov. 19, 2024.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois was elected vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus Wednesday, beating Rep. Sara Jacobs of California in a rare contested leadership race, 143-118.

Underwood, 40, is currently a co-chair of the caucus’ policy and communication arm and has served in leadership roles with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

She campaigned for the vice chair post leaning on her experience previously serving as a frontline member who flipped a Republican-held suburban Chicago seat in 2018. She boasted strong fundraising numbers and vowed to lead on Democratic messaging.

The vice chair position is effectively No. 6 on the Democratic leadership ladder. Races for the higher rungs were all uncontested.

item.title: Republican senator cancels vote on Trump pick to lead science foundation
item.description: Bill Cassidy said National Science Foundation nominee Jim O'Neill "did not do enough to stand up for science" as a Trump health official.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) canceled a vote for President Donald Trump's nominee to run the National Science Foundation.

item.dc:creator: By Chelsea Harvey
item.content:encoded:
The Republican chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee canceled a vote scheduled for Wednesday morning on Jim O’Neill’s nomination to lead the National Science Foundation, saying the former health official failed to stand up to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

O’Neill, a former government health official, would have been the first NSF director without a scientific or engineering background, which drew opposition from Democrats and science advocacy groups.

Committee Chair Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) cited O'Neill's stint as acting director of the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from August 2025 to February in canceling the nomination vote. “As acting CDC director, Mr. O’Neill did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy,” Cassidy said.

Cassidy also said O'Neill's role in firing the CDC's director, Dr. Susan Monarez, for failing to support Kennedy's questionable vaccine policies "raised further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF.”

“I like Jim personally,” Cassidy added. “But this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right.”

The scientific community widely opposed O’Neill’s nomination, citing his lack of scientific experience, his ties to Silicon Valley and his CDC record.

The nonprofit Stand Up for Science said it facilitated more than 1,000 calls and emails to Cassidy opposing O’Neill’s nomination in the past two days.

Gretchen Goldman, president of the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, said Tuesday that “NSF needs to be led by someone who can champion science for the public good and Jim O’Neill is not that person.”

The cancellation came after the HELP Committee had declined to hold a confirmation hearing for O’Neill, prompting Democratic senators to push to delay the vote on his nomination.

Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) sent a letter to Cassidy on Tuesday arguing that “the Senate should have an opportunity to hear directly from the nominee about how he would lead NSF.”

Stand Up for Science celebrated the canceled vote this morning, posting on Bluesky that “people power works.”

It’s unclear whether O’Neill’s nomination has been withdrawn or whether the vote has simply been postponed. Cassidy’s office did not immediately respond to inquiries about O’Neill’s nomination status.

item.title: Wes Moore cautions Dems against shutting down government over Iran war funding
item.description: The Maryland governor told POLITICO that Congress “should be able to” both bring an end to the war and keep the federal government open.

media:content.media:title: POLITICO's Megan Messerly speaks with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) at the POLITICO Pub during the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah, on Nov. 18, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Aaron Pellish
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore expressed frustration at the notion that Congress may shut down the government as Democrats push to tie a funding bill to cutting off Iran war funding.

Moore, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, told POLITICO that while he believes the Trump administration should end the war, the effort by some Democrats to add language to a government funding bill to end the war is misguided.

“I don't know why the American people are being asked to choose between ending a completely rudderless war that we're all paying for and saying, ‘Can we please keep the federal government open?’” Moore said at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah.

“I just think it's incredibly frustrating that once again we are being asked to be in this impossible position to say, 'End a ridiculous war or keep a federal government open,'” he added. “You should be able to do both.”

When asked if that meant he opposed using the government funding fight to try to force an end to the Trump administration’s military operations against Iran, Moore sharply criticized the Trump administration for launching the “absurd” conflict against Iran.

But the former Army officer who served in Afghanistan cited the importance of keeping the government funded for federal workers who would go without pay during a shutdown, many of whom reside in Maryland.

“As the governor of a state who's going to be impacted more than anybody else, I'm never going to say, ‘Yes, just shut down the government,’” he said. “I think it's ridiculous that Washington even has the ability to do it.”

Some Democrats in both chambers are pressuring leadership to draw a hard line on ending Iran war funding in any stopgap funding bill, which must be passed before the Dec. 11 deadline.

Moore also stressed the importance of keeping the government open in light of recent outages to government systems, including one that triggered a nationwide airplane ground stop last week, and attacked the Trump administration for laying off thousands of federal workers in 2025.

“You cannot separate what is happening with the federal government and these outages with the fact that it's our federal workers who've been fired,” he said.

item.title: Katherine Clark, Pete Aguilar, Joe Neguse elected to House majority posts
item.description: The Democratic leaders all won uncontested races by acclamation.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) speaks during a press conference at 55 M St. SE in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats filled out the top leadership echelon for their incoming majority Wednesday, promoting their current leaders in lockstep as expected.

Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts was elected majority leader, which will make her the first woman to hold the job of floor boss when Democrats take control in January.

Clark ran unopposed and won by acclamation in a closed-door caucus meeting.

House Democrats also elected Rep. Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip and Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker. Both, as with Clark, were unopposed and were elected by acclamation.

The leaders will work with the newly elected caucus chair, Rep. Ted Lieu of California, as well as speaker nominee Hakeem Jeffries of New York. All five have held similar leadership posts in the minority over the past four years.

The group is aligned in pursuing early votes on affordability and mounting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his administration.

item.title: Another rule vote pulled
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House GOP leaders have canceled a planned Wednesday vote to send two Republican-sponsored bills to the floor due to attendance issues, according to three people granted anonymity to describe internal decisionmaking.

The vote could be rescheduled for later in the week, but it puts passage of two labor-regulations bills — the American Franchise Act and the Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act — into doubt and reflects ongoing difficulties managing the thin GOP majority even after Election Day.

item.title: Trump’s FCC pick advances despite Democratic boycott
item.description: Democratic Senate Commerce Committee members skipped the vote in an attempt to protest Danielle Thumann Severs’ nomination.

media:content.media:title: The Senate Commerce Committee leaders have been at odds over advancing President Donald Trump's FCC nominee.

item.dc:creator: By John Hendel
item.content:encoded:
Senate Commerce Committee Republicans on Wednesday advanced President Donald Trump’s pick to fill an open Federal Communications Commission seat despite a Democratic boycott meant to obstruct the session.

The vote boosts the likelihood that Republicans confirm Danielle Thumann Severs in the lame duck while the party still controls the chamber. That confirmation would cement a deeper Republican majority at the telecom regulator and reduce the need for Trump to compromise and nominate Democrats next year.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called Democrats’ “temper tantrum” Wednesday a “terrible harbinger” heading into the new Congress.

Democrats view the nomination vote as a broader fight for the future of the five-member FCC, which typically is supposed to have members from both parties. But Democrats fear Trump could fire Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, if he is able to add Thumann Severs to the FCC since it would still have a quorum.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Senate Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said in a statement before the 10 a.m. scheduled start time.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr currently holds a 2-1 GOP majority, and he requires at least three members for a quorum to conduct much of the FCC's business.

“We made clear to Chairman Cruz that we had concerns about the nominee for the Federal Communications Commission being on the Executive Session until a Democratic nominee is put forward and asked that she be pulled from the markup,” Cantwell added. “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times. This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Cruz said the administration has recently made clear it will move Democratic nominees and maintained Republicans are still in the right to move nominations before them now.

Democrats also worry that Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to Carr, won’t be an independent voice on the commission. Carr has faced particularly intense criticism for how he has threatened and investigated media companies, including this year threatening the eight ABC station licenses of Disney and his scrutiny of TV hosts like Jimmy Kimmel.

item.title: Democrats overwhelmingly nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
item.description: He received an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York secured his fellow Democrats’ nomination Wednesday to lead the House, putting him on track to be elected the first Black speaker in January.

Jeffries, who has served in the House since 2013 and as minority leader since 2023, won the uncontested secret ballot 251-11 — an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

While some incoming members withheld their support, he chipped away at skeptics in private meetings and public policy commitments. His candidacy was buoyed by Democrats’ massive midterm victories that delivered a majority that could reach 260 seats once all votes are counted.

Several lawmakers representing different wings of the caucus spoke in favor of Jeffries before the vote, including progressive Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett from a Wisconsin swing district and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — previously the highest-ranking Black House Democrat before Jeffries’ ascension.

In his pitch to members, Jeffries, 56, leaned heavily on his record during two terms as party leader, highlighting Democrats’ resolve during shutdown fights and their success cornering Republicans through procedural maneuvers.

Progressives are enthused that Jeffries this week embraced lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding coverage to include vision, dental and hearing benefits, as well as establishing universal health coverage for children. Centrists have long backed Jeffries, cheering him as a pragmatic, consensus-oriented leader.

Some of the 11 holdouts issued a joint statement Wednesday acknowledging ongoing "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries but adding "there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The group of seven incoming members includes several self-identified democratic socialists, including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Melat Kiros of Colorado and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues," they said.

Jeffries has previewed that early votes under his leadership will include ending President Donald Trump’s tariffs, clawing back Republican-led Medicaid cuts and restoring expired Affordable Care Act tax credits.

He has also emphasized an oversight agenda that targets Trump, his administration and his allies, as well as anti-corruption measures such as a congressional stock trading ban.

item.title: Ted Lieu is elected House Democratic Caucus chair
item.description: He is set to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) speaks while Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries watches during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ted Lieu of California was elected House Democratic Caucus chair Wednesday morning in a closed-door meeting — the first of numerous leadership elections set to be decided this week.

Lieu, 57, won by acclamation in an uncontested bid for the post, meaning no official vote was tallied. He moves up from caucus vice chair and is now positioned to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

House Democrats will vote next on a nomination for speaker, where Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is uncontested, followed by elections for majority leader, whip and numerous junior caucus positions.

item.title: Bipartisan Senate duo urges ‘immediate’ White House action on AI-enabled cyber threats
item.description: Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds want leaders to harness existing federal agencies to counter major disruptions.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 8, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds called on the White House Tuesday night to “take immediate action” to protect against intensifying artificial-intelligence-juiced cyber threats against the nation’s infrastructure, financial institutions and software.

The bipartisan duo sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, chair of the recently formed “Superintelligence Task Force,” urging him to quickly bring together developers and federal experts to fully use the administration’s tools to counter cyber attacks plaguing banks and other systems.

“AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” wrote Cantwell of Washington, the top Democrat on Senate Commerce Committee, and Rounds of South Dakota, the chair of the Armed Services cybersecurity subcommittee. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday's cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

A spokesperson for Clayton did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new letter comes as the world faces credible threats of AI-enabled hacking targeting bank accounts and highly trafficked websites, jeopardizing personal and financial information worldwide.

Members of Congress are trying to figure out what to do about it, and the senators want Trump administration officials to use existing federal agencies and departments to fend off harm from models going rogue.

The letter urges the White House to direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to craft security standards for defensive AI agents and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to accelerate their adoption at banks, hospitals, utilities and government agencies.

The senators said the expertise within the federal government exists but that a coordinated approach is absent.

“The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort,” the senators wrote. “What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.”

As likely Commerce chair next year, Cantwell will have a new perch to push the administration and conduct oversight as she sees fit. Last month, she released a comprehensive framework that aims to tackle catastrophic risk and other problems.

item.title: US to reach $41T debt limit in February or March, forecasters predict
item.description: Reaching the borrowing cap will put an urgent to-do item on the agenda of the new Democrat-run Congress.

media:content.media:title: Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during the midterm convention.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
The United States is forecast to reach the $41.1 trillion debt limit in February or March, spurring a high-stakes fiscal policy debate during the early days of the Democrat-controlled Congress.

The Bipartisan Policy Center released that updated projection Wednesday, predicting that the federal government could get by for another six to nine months thereafter, since Treasury can deploy its usual cash-conservation tactics — known as “extraordinary measures” — once the debt limit is reached.

That means Congress’ drop-dead deadline for preventing a debt default, called the X-date, could fall sometime between August and December of next year.

The independent think tank, respected on Capitol Hill for its accurate forecasting of the debt limit in years past, noted that U.S. debt has risen faster than projected since last year, in part because the Trump administration is raking in less cash than expected from tariffs.

Democratic lawmakers have already started discussing the possibility of raising the debt limit through the party-line reconciliation process, like their GOP counterparts did last year.

That would spare the new majority party from having to strike up bipartisan negotiations with President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers, under pressure from fiscal conservatives to demand spending limits as a condition of allowing the nation to take on more red ink.

item.title: Garcia gives Trump allies early warning on the investigations to come
item.description: Democrats plan to use their new power to investigate the White House’s role in the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and Trump family business dealings.

media:content.media:title: House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.dc:contributor: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats are signaling their top investigative targets in the new Congress, starting with President Donald Trump’s family members and closest aides — from sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump to chief of staff Stephen Miller, former chief Susie Wiles and Vice President JD Vance.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to be the next chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent letters to all five Wednesday morning, indicating they will be subjects of interest to the panel next year as he prepares to make good on his promise to probe Trump family business ties, ICE’s mass deportation campaign, the administration’s handling of the Epstein files and more.

The California Democrat sent a total of 12 letters to high-profile figures in Trump’s orbit, including Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, Attorney General Todd Blanche and former ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, as well as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her former adviser Corey Lewandowski. The letters, which have no legal force, urge the recipients to preserve documents in anticipation of the investigations Democrats plan to launch when they take over the House in January. And they provide the clearest early window into the soon-to-be-majority’s most pressing investigative priorities.

It’s a sign the incoming Democratic majority will not shy away from confrontations with the White House that could lead to court battles likely to drag on for the remainder of Trump’s term. Administrations of both parties have typically treated senior White House officials — especially chiefs of staff like Miller and Wiles — as immune from compelled testimony to Congress.

The letters are an answer to the Trump administration’s recent warnings about potential criminal prosecution of Democrats who engage in oversight activities it considers “weaponized” or overly punitive.

The White House and Justice Department also have repeatedly warned of possible criminal investigations for demands they consider out of bounds — or lacking a “legitimate legislative task,” as longstanding precedents require. Garcia’s 12 letters nod to that requirement, each including a line describing the investigations as “essential for legislative reform.”

“As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though some letters request responses by December, Democrats don’t yet have the power to compel answers. And even when they do, congressional oversight requests — including subpoena deadlines — are typically flexible and depend on the targets’ willingness to negotiate and cooperate.

Here’s what Oversight Committee Democrats are most interested in pursuing come January:

Trump family business dealings

Garcia is signaling that Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump will be the subjects of an inquiry into their roles as co-founders of World Liberty Financial, a Trump family cryptocurrency business. The committee’s top Democrat describes the brothers as key players in “the Trump family’s pay-to-play schemes” which “have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years.” A World Liberty Financial spokesperson has previously said “no one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government” and the company is compliant with all U.S. laws.

Donald Trump Jr. is also under scrutiny in connection with his elaborate wedding celebration that was funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin. Kremlev has said the younger Trump paid him back. Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina Trump wrote in a social media post that the celebration was an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” that had been “recast as something political or sinister.”

“Foreign interests also funded your lavish wedding celebrations, raising further concerns of pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the Trump family,” Garcia said. “These associations may have already benefited special interests, but they have not helped the American people.”

Democrats also have their sights on Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a U.S. special envoy, for his personal business dealings and government work. Garcia raised concerns that “hundreds of millions of dollars in management fees, business opportunities, and other financial benefits are serving as disguised payoffs for policy changes, preferential treatment, relief from legal scrutiny, and access to sensitive government information and technology.” Kushner has repeatedly denied leveraging his powerful father-in-law for personal gain.

"These allegations have it exactly backwards. Jared Kushner has always acted in the best interests of the United States,” Chad Mizelle, Kushner’s attorney, said. “He has voluntarily stepped away from his successful business to devote his time, without compensation, to helping President Trump end wars, save lives, and advance American interests. Any suggestion that he has used his public service for personal financial gain is categorically false."

The White House has repeatedly denied that Trump or his family members have engaged in any conflicts of interest. The Trump brothers did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia also wrote to Catherine Townsend, CEO of the Trust for the National Mall, inquiring about donations by private entities and companies to support Trump’s White House ballroom. Among the companies named is the embattled chip manufacturer Nvidia, which Garcia notes “donated millions to the Trust for the National Mall shortly after receiving permission from the Trump Administration to sell advanced microchips to the People’s Republic of China.”

Nvidia has maintained its donation was made independently of any potential business interests. The Trust for the National Mall said in a statement the organization's "limited role was to receive and manage charitable donations" and "had no role in fundraising or soliciting donations or in design or construction of the project." The organization said it plans to cooperate with congressional inquiries related to the project.

Immigration enforcement

Garcia also outlined the panel’s plans to investigate “the violence, abuse, and corruption carried out by the Department of Homeland Security” under Miller’s direction. The committee said it has found 1,165 instances of concerning uses of force, arrests, deportations and enforcement actions at sensitive locations and other “acts of intimidation or retaliation.”

“Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the ‘linchpin’ and ‘architect’ of the Trump Administration’s most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties,” Garcia wrote to Miller, now Trump’s chief of staff. “We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses.”

Garcia also pledged to investigate allegations that Noem “abused DHS funds, undermined career employees, circumvented established safeguards that prevent corruption, and used your position to enrich yourself and associates of the Trump Administration.”

The letter to Noem also makes note of her role running an agency that presided over “pay-to-play schemes conducted” by Lewandowski, her former employee at DHS who is also being probed by the committee for alleged kickbacks from GEO Group, a company that runs private detention facilities for migrants. Lewandowski has previously denied demanding payments from the company.

“Congressman Garcia’s attempts to build a misleading narrative about Mr. Lewandowski as part of his party’s campaign against the current administration will be proven false at the appropriate time and in the appropriate forum,” a spokesperson for Lewandowski said.

Noem was forced out of DHS in March after facing intense scrutiny inside the White House and calls from some GOP lawmakers to resign over her management of the department.

Noem did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Epstein files

Garcia is also probing the administration’s handling of the investigative materials related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the web of people and institutions who allegedly aided his crimes.

In a letter to Vance, Garcia asked the vice president to identify every meeting officials had on the Epstein files, citing reports outlining Vance’s role in the conversations. Garcia is also seeking information related to the administration’s response to the law Congress passed last year mandating the files’ public disclosure, which lawmakers in both parties have panned as incomplete.

Justice Department officials have said they did their best to follow the law’s disclosure requirements and have sought to correct any errors or address victims’ concerns, but Democrats are still clamoring for sworn testimony from Blanche, who had a key role in overseeing the files’ release.

Garcia is also demanding information about the decision to move Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein's co-conspirator, to a lower security federal prison where she’s serving a 20-year sentence.

He wrote to Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall III as well as to Tanisha Hall — the warden of Federal Prison Camp Bryan who runs the minimum security facility where Maxwell was moved — to get answers about Maxwell’s transfer after the Justice Department and the Bureau of Prisons “failed to meaningfully respond to any of our inquiries.”

Marshall and Hall did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia is, in addition, asking Wiles — Trump’s former chief of staff — and Blanche for information related to the Epstein saga. Wiles was also unreachable for comment.

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

item.title: ‘Looks a lot different now’: Black Democrats are no longer in lockstep on seniority
item.description: Divisions on committee term limits come at a moment of triumph for the powerful Congressional Black Caucus.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.) is challenging a fellow CBC member for the Education and Labor gavel.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson and Mackenzie Wilkes
item.dc:contributor: By Riley Rogerson and Mackenzie Wilkes
item.content:encoded:
The Congressional Black Caucus has long served as the top champion for House Democrats’ strict seniority system, beating back multiple attempts to encourage turnover in the top party echelon.

Now the calls for generational change inside the party are coming from within its own ranks.

Several long-tenured Black committee leaders are looking to get their gavels back when Democrats retake the majority in January. They include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who is 78; Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, who is 79; and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who is 88. All have served at least a decade atop their respective committees — Homeland Security, Education and Workforce, and Financial Services.

But many newer and some senior members are saying they’re open to supporting term limits, defying a longstanding CBC position in favor of seniority that defenders say has been the cornerstone of Black power on Capitol Hill. Multiple committee leaders are facing insurgent challengers, with Scott staring down a contest with a fellow CBC member, Rep. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut.

“Debate is always a good thing,” Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama said in an interview, acknowledging the difference of opinions in the caucus. “CBC looks a lot different now than it did 10 years ago, let alone 20 or 30 years ago.”

The newly emerging divisions inside the CBC on the term-limits issue come at a moment of triumph for the powerful caucus. Its ranks will swell to more than 60 members next year after Black candidates defied Republican attempts to eliminate minority-majority districts with mid-cycle redistricting.

The debate is expected to play out over the next two weeks ahead of a caucus rules vote in early December. Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada is proposing to establish a four-term limit on committee leadership, which would force Scott, Thompson and Waters out of their posts after the coming Congress unless they seek a waiver. The same would be true for Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, who leads Democrats on Foreign Affairs.

The evolving perspectives inside the CBC are one reason, many observers say, that a Democratic term limits proposal could actually be adopted this year. Republicans have had a three-term limit for their committee leaders in place for more than 30 years, though waivers have been granted in some circumstances allowing members to serve longer.

Meeks, a former CBC chair, and Rep. Yvette Clarke of New York, the current chair, oppose committee term limits, evoking well-known and previously effective arguments that minority members can find it harder to pull key levers of internal power — such as fundraising — and that seniority is an effective equalizer.

“I think the voters make the determination on term limits,” Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina said in an interview. “I think that we have to protect seniority in this place.”

Clyburn, for years the highest-ranking Black leader in Congress, has also noted in the past that Black lawmakers of his generation had to work harder to get elected to office, meaning they often started later in their careers than their white counterparts.

But that seniority principle no longer enjoys near-universal agreement in the caucus ranks. In a sign of the sea change, CBC member and presumptive speaker Hakeem Jeffries is letting the term-limits debate play out, last week calling it “the right conversation to have.”

“Like anything else, members of the CBC have different ideas,” said Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is running unopposed to lead the caucus next year. “We're not a monolith, and we encourage people to have their own thoughts and ideas.”

For all the clout it affords the most veteran Democrats, the seniority system can seem daunting to younger members who face the prospect of having to serve a decade or more before winning a gavel on a choice committee. And some new and existing CBC members are speaking out.

“I think it should be considered,” Rep.-elect La Shawn Ford of Illinois said in an interview about term limits for committee leaders. “You do want experienced people on leading committees, but I don't think that it should be the only factor that determines a chair vote.”

The internal debate has been dramatically underscored by Hayes’ run against Scott for the top job on the Education and Workforce Committee, which is likely to be renamed Education and Labor under Democratic control.

“I understand why CBC had long-held positions because things had not been fair for a very long time,” Hayes said in an interview. But, she added, “the caucus is getting bigger and bigger, and people come with different backgrounds and different perspectives.“

Clarke said the CBC is unlikely to wade into the Hayes vs. Scott race, explaining that the caucus doesn’t typically endorse in committee chair contests. (Rep. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, who is not a member of the CBC, is also running for the Education gavel and has vowed to serve no more than four years).

But last month, Clarke issued a statement of support for Waters, who is seeking an eighth term leading Democrats on the Financial Services Committee against a bid from Rep. Sean Casten of Illinois. She said the CBC is “unwavering in its support” of the longtime leader.

At least one CBC member, Rep. Shontel Brown of Ohio, is running for a vacant role atop the Agriculture Committee against the more senior Rep. Jim Costa of California. A second, Rep. Don Davis of North Carolina, has talked to colleagues about running.

While the debate is breaking down on perhaps predictable generational lines, there are some complications to that narrative.

Rep.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado said in an interview she is supporting Waters’ bid to remain atop the Financial Services panel past her 90th birthday, while also saying “term limits are important so that we can start building the bench.”

“I think term limits are important, and I think it's also important that we make sure that we're still seeing representation on a lot of these different committees,” she said.

Some longtime members, meanwhile, are at least open to a debate.

Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey is retiring after 12 years in the House. Much of that she spent on the Appropriations Committee, where she never even led a subcommittee. (She did chair a Homeland Security subcommittee at one point.)

“I see both sides — I really see the value of institutional knowledge and experience,” she said, pointing to Thompson’s service atop Homeland Security and the Jan. 6 select committee.

But she pointed to two younger members — Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Robert Garcia of California — who beat out more seasoned members to take over the Judiciary and Oversight panels, respectively.

“It kind of works out sometimes,” she said.

item.title: Democrats on House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs probing Lutnick family’s role in Nvidia scandal
item.description: Reps. Jamie Raskin and Greg Meeks are also investigating the Commerce Secretary’s old firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

media:content.media:title: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick arrives for an American mining industry roundtable at State Department headquarters in Washington, D.C. on Aug. 7, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees are launching a probe into whether the Trump administration’s response to Nvidia’s alleged chip smuggling into Beijing was influenced by the significant shares that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s family holds in the company.

It comes amid the larger fallout from allegations that Nvidia’s ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who was, in turn, accused of funneling advanced chips to China through the firm Megaspeed. It also provides a window into how the incoming chairs of Judiciary and Foreign Affairs — Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Gregory Meeks of New York, respectively — plan to leverage their new majority in January to advance existing lines of inquiry into this episode.

That includes shining a spotlight on Lutnick, who is also coming under scrutiny for appearing too close to Huang and not doing enough to crack down on Nvidia’s chip sales to China — including by leaving Megaspeed off a list of companies deemed national security risks.

Raskin, Meeks and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.), another signatory on the letter, want to know whether there’s any connection between those accusations against Lutnick and the fact that he previously held more than $1.3 billion in Nvidia stock through the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, which he ran until he transferred ownership to his children at the time of his confirmation in 2025.

“If these media reports are accurate, the American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” Raskin and Meeks said in a letter dated Nov. 17 to Brandon Lutnick, who is currently serving as the firm’s chair.

“Secretary Lutnick’s reported obstruction may have resulted in billions of dollars of restricted AI chips being diverted to China,” the lawmakers continued. “It also propped up the prices of NVIDIA for months, preventing devastating losses for your company, which not only held a substantial position in NVIDIA, but strongly encouraged its clients to buy NVIDIA stock.”

Meeks, Raskin and Kamlager-Dove told Brandon Lutnick they want all communications with Cantor Fitzgerald clients referring to U.S. export control changes on advanced semiconductors, including with respect to Nvidia customers like Megaspeed. They’re also asking for all information concerning personal investments or other financial interests in Nvidia by Howard Lutnick and President Donald Trump along with documents showing every trade involving Nvidia stock executed by Cantor Fitzgerald between Jan. 1, 2024 to the present.

“Failure to preserve relevant materials could impede congressional oversight and any subsequent investigation. We therefore request written confirmation by 5:00 p.m. on December 1, 2026, that Cantor Fitzgerald has implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records,” the lawmakers wrote.


Danielle Popper, a spokesperson for Cantor Fitzgerald, called the claims made by the letter “inaccurate” and maintained the firm is “in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations.”

“Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” Popper said in a statement. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. We buy the underlying shares to hedge those trades. The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position.”

She added that “allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless” and that “Cantor has no role in U.S. export control or Entity List decisions.”

A spokesperson for the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

While Democrats have no means or authority to compel the release of this information now, they are laying the groundwork for early next year, when Raskin and Meeks will have the ability to deploy subpoenas to access certain information and force people to testify.

item.title: Murkowski faces real challenge in bid to be top GOP appropriator
item.description: Two GOP senators predicted Republicans on the committee would support Sen. Jerry Moran, who is challenging her for the position.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Lisa Murkowski arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on March 20.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney, Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney, Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski is facing a serious challenge in her bid to lead Republicans on the Appropriations Committee next year.

Many expected it to be a foregone conclusion that the Alaska lawmaker would succeed outgoing chair Susan Collins of Maine, who lost her reelection earlier this month; Murkowski is currently the most senior member of the GOP side of the committee dais eligible for a promotion.

But two Republican senators, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said they currently expect GOP members of the Senate Appropriations Committee to instead pick Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kansas) as the party’s vice-chair.

“Moran will win,” said one of the senators in an interview Tuesday regarding the anticipated outcome of the committee vote.

Republicans on the Appropriations Committee won’t have the final say — and it’s still early in the discussions about who will get top Senate committee slots. But opting to effectively bless leapfrogging Murkowski in favor of Moran would be an astounding move for a conference that has long relied on seniority to determine who gets to lead the GOP on committees.

Republican appropriators will vote in January, once new GOP senators are added to the panel, for who they want leading them on the committee. That is, however, only a recommendation that has to then be upheld by the full Senate Republican Conference.

And it’s not clear, currently, how the full Senate GOP conference would handle a recommendation to set aside Murkowski as the top Republican on the panel, according to the two Senate Republicans as well as an additional GOP senator and two aides with knowledge of the matter — also granted anonymity to speak candidly given the sensitivity of the race.

The third senator said they weren’t yet sure who would win the vote among Appropriations Committee Republicans, but that they had advised Moran to “touch base with his leadership team … because the implications to losing a chairmanship also means bigger things for the conference.”

The ramifications, some Republicans worry, could involve a scenario where more GOP senators feel empowered to challenge more senior members for committee leadership spots, prompting open warfare as the party is still trying to regroup after a bruising election cycle. It would also just mark a deviation from the way the conference typically does business — though the conference rules don’t require that the top spot for a committee also be the most senior member.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said last week he hadn’t yet weighed into the dispute between Murkowski and Moran but that he had advised them to “talk it out” and that “we’ll see where those conversations lead.”

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), a member of leadership and a high-ranking appropriator, said Tuesday she didn’t know what the outcome of the contest would be but that Murkowski and Moran will meet this week.

Murkowski and Moran have in the meantime both been privately meeting with, and making the case to, colleagues. Spokespeople for neither of the two GOP senators provided a request for comment Tuesday.

Moran did not articulate to POLITICO last week a reason for why he would challenge Murkowski. She will, however, be the most moderate GOP senator remaining come January, and has broken with her party on numerous high-profile decisions over the years.

Democrats also view Murkowski as someone they could potentially negotiate with on government spending deals but are staying out of the GOP dispute.

“Boy, that’s an [intra]party fight on that side. You know, I would have to say on our side that would be really hard, where somebody who’s done all the work and moved their way up — but that’s their neighborhood,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), who will chair the committee next year, said in an interview.

Also potentially working to Murkowski’s disadvantage is that Republicans will be losing five senators on the Appropriations Committee come January, many of whom would have likely been Murkowski allies. It’s not yet clear who will get their spots and who Murkowski and Moran will need to win over.

And even as Republicans grapple with Murkowski’s fate, they appear poised to let GOP senators who have infuriated their colleagues over the past year hold top committee spots. Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rand Paul of Kentucky — two notorious thorns in leadership’s side — are, respectively, on tap to be ranking members on the Judiciary Committee and the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions panel.

Neither man currently has a challenger seeking to bypass the seniority system.
